tools.name: read
tools.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

anyOf.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)
Maximum number of lines to read

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB. If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Supports standard input via stdin and background execution via run_in_background: true.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

stdin.description: Optional standard input to pass to the command

run_in_background.description: Run command in background detached from the current turn. Returns immediately with task ID.

verbatim.description: Run command verbatim without RTK output compression or rewriting. Use when exact raw output or unfiltered flags are required.

expect.description: The exit status you predict for a foreground command: success (exit 0) or failure. The result reports a surprise when the prediction misses.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

tools.name: revisit_note
tools.description: Revisit one specific entry in the session notebook and recover the conversation, commands, or file changes behind it. Use the 12-character id shown beside a working conclusion or archived note when its summary is too compressed to rely on confidently. This follows a known note back to its sources; it does not search the transcript by topic.

id.description: The 12-character lowercase hex id shown beside a working conclusion or archived note in the compacted notebook, /pair notebook, or a previous revisit_note result. This tool follows a known note; it does not search by topic.

tools.name: update_notebook
tools.description: Record, supersede, or retire learnings in the notebook you share with the pair programmer. A learning is something found out the hard way and what to do differently now. Each cites source entry ids, or the current user turn when sourceEntryIds is omitted. Retire a learning with retireReflectionIds once its durable owner holds it or it is not worth keeping.

sourceEntryIds.description: Primary source entry ids. Omit to cite the current user turn.

tools.name: acknowledge_pair_findings
tools.description: Record that you considered one or more delivered pair programmer concerns or blockers. Use address when acting on a finding, decline when evidence shows it does not apply, or defer when it is valid but outside the authorized work. Give a concise reason. This records consideration only; it does not claim the work is fixed or validated.

tools.name: ask_user_question
tools.description: Ask the user one to 4 related structured questions instead of guessing. Each question must offer 2-4 authored choices with concise labels and descriptions. The UI automatically adds a custom free-text answer. Set multiSelect when more than one authored choice can apply.

question.description: The complete, specific question to show the user

header.description: Short tab label, such as Scope or Storage

label.description: Concise display label for this choice (prefer 1-5 words)

description.description: What this choice means, including its main consequence or trade-off

options.description: Distinct authored choices. The custom-answer choice is appended automatically.

multiSelect.description: Allow more than one authored choice to be selected

questions.description: One to four related questions to ask in one questionnaire

tools.name: search_session
tools.description: Search this session's earlier conversation, tool calls, and write/edit payloads. Use it after compaction when you need to remember a prior decision, recover earlier tool output, or revisit a file version written during the session. This looks through session history, not git history or the current repository. Search text or regex, list touched files, inspect only write/edit payloads, expand entries, recover a written file with query:'#N:path', or recover an omitted tool result with query:'call:<id>'. Expand any source by query:'entry:<id>[:offset[:limit]]' (zero-based lines). New custom, summary and notebook records use stable IDs, not message ordinals. It follows the active lineage by default; scope:'all' includes other branches. Natural-language history discovery uses the runtime's index. Use tasks:[id] to search what people wrote while focused on those authorized tasks; task queries match words, not regex patterns, and punctuation is ignored. Use fields:'words' to omit tool payloads from indexed discovery. Other people's sources use entry:<session>/<id>[:offset[:limit]]. Runtime failures/refusals are reported, not replaced with another engine.

tasks.description: Search these tasks' focus spans across their workers. Requires task access. History queries match words, not regex patterns; punctuation is ignored. A span means written while focused, not necessarily about the task.

fields.description: Indexed discovery: words searches written text, thinking, mail and summaries; all (default) also searches tool calls and results.

query.description: Search text or regex (e.g. 'hook|inject'); multi-word terms are OR-ranked. Recover written content with '#N:path[:offset[:limit]|:full]', or an omitted tool result with 'call:<toolCallId>' from a pair receipt.

expand.description: Non-negative entry indices to return full untruncated content for. Works alone (any index in scope) or alongside query (expands matching entries on the current page).

page.description: Positive page number (1-based) for paginated search results. Default: 1.

mode.description: history (default), file (write/edit payload search only), or touched (files grouped by path).

scope.description: Search scope. Options: 'lineage' (default) or 'all' (entire session, including branches).

tools.name: repo_rules
tools.description: Read-only: list this repository's rules in .pi/rules/ (comment policy, GritQL code rules, action rules) with how many times each has refused a change or command and when it last did. Use it to narrow a rule that blocks good code or retire one that never fires.

tools.name: tlc_check
tools.description: Model-check a TLA+ specification with TLC and get a structured verdict: pass (every reachable state checked), violation (with the violated invariant or property), deadlock, incomplete (a time limit, simulation or depth bound stopped the search first, with the counts reached), or error. A failure returns the counterexample as numbered states, each with its action and variable values. Every run lists the actions that never took a step. The spec may extend other modules in its directory and the TLA+ Community Modules (SequencesExt, FiniteSetsExt, Functions, Folds, Relation, Graphs and more). Downloads pinned, checksummed tools on first use; needs Java.

config.description: Path to the .cfg file; defaults to the spec's .cfg

mode.description: exhaustive (default): breadth-first over every reachable state. simulate: random behaviors. depth-first: every behavior up to `depth` steps

constants.description: Constant values in .cfg syntax (a number, string, model value, or set of them), replacing the .cfg's

timeLimit.description: Seconds before TLC stops and reports what it reached

workers.description: TLC worker threads; defaults to every core (depth-first supports only 1)

depth.description: depth-first: the bound on behavior length. simulate: the longest behavior (TLC default 100)

traces.description: simulate: how many behaviors to generate

seed.description: simulate: the random seed, to repeat a run

tools.name: tla_symbolic_check
tools.description: Check a TLA+ specification symbolically with Apalache (SMT), without enumerating states: integers need no bounds, constants can range over whole sets such as Nat, and an inductive invariant proves a property for behaviors of any length. Returns the same verdicts as tlc_check: pass, violation with its counterexample trace, deadlock, incomplete, or error. Downloads a pinned, checksummed Apalache (192 MB) on first use; needs Java 17.

config.description: Path to a TLC-format .cfg; defaults to the spec's .cfg when it exists

mode.description: bounded (default): every behavior up to `length` steps. inductive: a proof for every length

invariants.description: Invariants to check or prove; defaults to the .cfg's INVARIANT

length.description: bounded: the most steps to check (default 10)

constInit.description: Operator that assigns the constants, such as ConstInit == N \in Nat

checkDeadlock.description: bounded: report deadlock; defaults to the .cfg's CHECK_DEADLOCK, else on

tools.name: pi_exec
tools.description: Run type-checked Python in bounded Monty to compose tools and HTTP requests, and compute over their results. Return a JSON-compatible trailing expression; printed output is also captured. See code for live signatures and runtime constraints. Managing roles can also delegate peer turns.

code.description:
Python 3.14 subset (Monty). Snippets accept top-level await and return the trailing expression. All code is type-checked before execution.
Import asyncio and use asyncio.gather(*awaitables) for independent fan-out; await dependent steps in order. There is no create_task and no third-party import.
Host functions are async; pass keyword arguments. schema(shape) is pure local Python. Type-checking stubs:
from typing import Any, Literal, NotRequired, TypedDict
inputs: dict[str, str]
class EditEditsItem(TypedDict):
    oldText: str
    newText: str
async def read(*, path: str, offset: float = ..., limit: float = ...) -> str: ...
async def grep(*, pattern: str, path: str = ..., glob: str = ..., ignoreCase: bool = ..., literal: bool = ..., context: float = ..., limit: float = ...) -> str: ...
async def find(*, pattern: str, path: str = ..., limit: float = ...) -> str: ...
async def ls(*, path: str = ..., limit: float = ...) -> str: ...
async def bash(*, command: str, timeout: float = ..., stdin: str = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def edit(*, path: str, edits: list[EditEditsItem]) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def write(*, path: str, content: str) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
def schema(shape: Any) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
class Peer:
    async def run(self, task: str, *, output_schema: dict[str, Any] | None = ...) -> Any: ...
    async def close(self) -> None: ...
async def peer(role: str) -> Peer: ...
peers: dict[str, Peer]
async def agent_run(*, role: str, task: str, name: str = ..., context: Any = ..., output_schema: dict[str, Any] = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def agent(*, role: str, task: str, name: str = ..., context: Any = ..., output_schema: dict[str, Any] = ...) -> Any: ...
async def tools_list() -> list[dict[str, Any]]: ...
async def tools_search(query: str) -> list[dict[str, Any]]: ...
async def tools_describe(name: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None: ...
async def tools_call(name: str, args: dict[str, Any] = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def skills_list() -> list[dict[str, str]]: ...
async def skills_body(name: str) -> str: ...
async def fetch(url: str, *, method: str = ..., headers: dict[str, str] = ..., body: str | bytes = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def git_change(*, target: dict[str, str] = ..., paths: list[str] = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def git_patch(*, target: dict[str, str] = ..., paths: list[str] = ...) -> str: ...
async def repo_change_neighborhood(*, target: dict[str, str] = ..., paths: list[str] = ..., include: list[str] = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def context_required(*, value: Any) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def context_clippable(*, value: str, max_chars: int = ..., strategy: str = ..., marker: str = ..., priority: float = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def context_droppable(*, value: Any, priority: float = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def context_fit(*, value: Any, max_serialized_chars: int = ..., flags: dict[str, str] = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def context_pack(*, items: list[Any], id: str = ..., priority: str = ..., fields: dict[str, int] = ..., max_serialized_chars: int = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def dev_find_relevant_tests(*, target: dict[str, str] = ..., paths: list[str] = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
async def dev_run_relevant_tests(*, target: dict[str, str] = ..., paths: list[str] = ..., command: str = ..., max_tests: int = ..., timeout: float = ...) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
Captured extension tools are async functions here too, with keyword arguments type-checked against their schemas. Find one with tools_list() or tools_search(query) and read its parameters with await tools_describe(name="...").
tools_search/tools_call support dynamic discovery. fetch handles HTTP; skills_list/skills_body expose model-invocable skills.
git_change/git_patch and repo_change_neighborhood collect scoped evidence for target={"kind": "working-tree", "base": "HEAD"} by default, the same target shapes as review_code (staged, commit, range, branch); context_* fits structured evidence; dev_find_relevant_tests/dev_run_relevant_tests locate and run focused checks.
agent_run returns a status record (including errors, and per-file edit/write changes); agent returns text or the output_schema value and raises on failure. Both create a fresh catalog-role peer, assign the goal, and discard the peer when the call ends. Context is bound as a file beside that goal, not copied into its text. Use schema({"id": "int"}) for strict object schemas.
Inputs is a dict of caller-supplied strings. Python globals persist across calls on the current Pi session branch and keep their first type, so give each program's variables specific names; reset is a tool parameter that starts fresh. bash, edit, and write return {"ok": bool, "output": str}. Print is captured. Return only JSON-compatible values; display and limits are tool parameters, not globals.

inputs.description: Named strings available to the program as inputs.<key>.

peers.description: Named awake colleagues: map names to session ids, then await peers[name].run(task). Attached sessions stay alive; the program owns only its requested turns.

reset.description: Start a fresh Monty session on this branch before running the snippet.

display.description: Tool-call metadata for the live card and activity widget. Not a program global; pass display outside code.

agentBudget.description: Max peer turns for this program, including attached colleagues and reused handles.

callBudget.description: Max host calls for this program.

concurrency.description: Max in-flight host calls. Excess work queues.

timeoutSeconds.description: Wall-clock seconds before the program is stopped.

limits.description: Optional capacity for this program. Omitted fields keep the shape-derived default. Values clamp to package maxima.

tools.name: resolve_finding
tools.description: Append an accountable finding response to a settled captured assessment. Supply its current revision and digest from read_review. Rejection needs counterevidence; accepted risk needs evidence and explicit scope. A claimed fix remains unverified. Fixed requires a specific completed, unchallenged question on a different captured target and supporting evidence; this records your judgment, not a correctness certificate. A fix in later code never changes the original snapshot. Responses retain the original allegation and invalidate older assessment approval. Only the operator can approve code through sign-off.

review.description: A returned review ID, or the request handle of its admission. Access follows the recorded organization.

digest.description: Exact artifact digest from the current summary.

request.description: Replay the exact earlier request using its returned handle. Changed arguments are refused. Omit for a new request.

tools.name: review_code
tools.description: Capture an exact commit, range, branch, staged index or working tree and enqueue independent semantic/risk-based review through ordinary role peers. This starts model work under the configured role profiles. Return after target capture and admission, not after review. The author's index and checkout stay unchanged. Supply approved intent when available; absent intent stays unassessed. The owner (you, by default) receives mail when the plan is ready, as each pass's findings are confirmed, and when the review settles; keep working and course-correct as findings arrive, or pass wait to block until it settles and get the outcome in the result instead of the mail. Exact request replay retains the original captured target even if the checkout changes.

target.description: The change: {"kind":"working-tree","base":"HEAD"} for tracked, staged and untracked edits against an exact base; {"kind":"staged"} for the index against HEAD; {"kind":"commit","commit":"X"} for one commit against its parent (merges need "parent"); {"kind":"range","base":"A","head":"B"} for exact endpoints; {"kind":"branch","base":"main","head":"feature"} for feature since its merge base with main, as a pull request shows it.

cwd.description: Repository or worktree directory; defaults to the current session directory.

owner.description: Existing lasting person's ID. Omit to own the review yourself; assigning another owner requires management authority.

parent.description: Earlier review ID whose evidence this new capture follows; it grants no coverage credit.

request.description: Replay the exact earlier request using its returned handle. Changed arguments are refused. Omit for a new request.

wait.description: Block until the review settles, then return its summary and confirmed findings. Its milestone mail then arrives only as a pointer. Omit to keep working; mail reports each validated pass's findings and the outcome as they happen.

tools.name: review_queue
tools.description: Inspect the durable review queue in your organization. Without limit, return state counts; with limit, return a page of meaningful status, coverage, findings and captured-target identity. Active work precedes queued priority/FIFO work and history. Reported cost covers retained primary turns across all attempts, including failures; missing observations stay explicit. Completion is not approval or proof of correctness. These reads do not establish current-checkout freshness.

limit.description: Requested page size. Omit for counts; there is no implicit detail-page budget.

offset.description: Row offset; requires limit. Pages observe current state, not a frozen queue.

cwd.description: Filter a recorded repository or requested worktree directory.

hideAddressed.description: Leave out settled reviews whose confirmed findings all have a response; they need nothing more from anyone.

analytics.description: Return cost and yield instead of the queue: totals, by model, by phase and per review, from recorded usage.

tools.name: read_review
tools.description: Read one captured review progressively. Summary separates execution, missing intent, question coverage, findings and reported primary-turn cost across all attempts. Cost excludes unobserved internal activity; missing observations and unavailable totals stay explicit. Freshness explicitly rechecks the requested target, current checkout and recorded review policy at a stated time; changed or unavailable is not current, and this read never transfers coverage/approval. Configuration shows captured review instructions and declared model/profile references, not a frozen ambient environment; actual role/model policy belongs to each attempt. Target gives captured source and Git revisions; ordinary tools remain available there. Source browses retained Git objects on the before or after side: omit path to list files, or name a captured file to read lines. It never follows symlinks or automatically appends .context sidecars; inspect captured context files and applicable docs separately. Source and the other collections return counts until limit is supplied; source file offsets are zero-based line offsets. Plan, changes, regions, findings, coverage and attempts also page explicitly. Pass requires its pass ID; attempt requires its attempt ID and exposes that retained input policy, raw result, observed turn usage and validated output. Thread pages the review's mail (milestones and comments). Log shows the recent transcript of the running passes, or of one attempt. Original allegations and validation remain distinct. These reads establish neither freshness nor approval.

review.description: A returned review ID, or the request handle of its admission. Access follows the recorded organization.

path.description: Captured repository-relative file path for part: source. Omit to list files.

side.description: Captured comparison side for part: source; defaults to after.

pass.description: Pass ID from the plan; required for part: pass.

attempt.description: Attempt ID from the attempts page or selected pass; required for part: attempt.

limit.description: Requested page size. Omit for counts; there is no implicit detail-page budget.

offset.description: Row offset; requires limit. Pages observe current state, not a frozen queue.

wait.description: Block until the review settles, then return its summary and confirmed findings. Its milestone mail then arrives only as a pointer. Omit to keep working; mail reports each validated pass's findings and the outcome as they happen.

tools.name: manage_review
tools.description: Cancel unfinished review work and wait for guarded cleanup, explicitly resume interrupted/failed/incomplete work on the same verified artifact, reprioritize queued work, reassign responsibility, or rerun the original capture request as a new review linked to this one (owned by you unless owner is supplied). Resume checks current role/profile policy before reusing exact-input work. A changed policy or advisory catalog requires a new plan and fresh inspections; challenged or incomplete work also reruns. Rerun resolves mutable targets again and grants no old coverage credit. Extend explicitly authorizes a concrete additional question with its reason and doneWhen evidence on the same retained target, bound to the current revision/digest. It replans required work and can incur new model cost; old attempts remain history, not automatic coverage credit. Resume alone is not a waiver or authorization of new questions.

review.description: A returned review ID, or the request handle of its admission. Access follows the recorded organization.

priority.description: Queue priority; higher values precede lower ones. Required for priority.

owner.description: Existing lasting person's ID; required for reassign, optional for rerun.

revision.description: Current assessment revision; required for extend.

digest.description: Captured target digest; required for extend.

question.description: Concrete additional review question; required for extend.

reason.description: Why additional work is justified; required for extend.

doneWhen.description: Evidence that settles this question; required for extend.

request.description: Replay the exact earlier request using its returned handle. Changed arguments are refused. Omit for a new request.

wait.description: Block until the review settles, then return its summary and confirmed findings. Its milestone mail then arrives only as a pointer. Omit to keep working; mail reports each validated pass's findings and the outcome as they happen.

tools.name: explore
tools.description: Ask a cheap intern to map local code or investigate the filesystem. A cheap intern is fast and keeps reading out of your context, but returns a lossy summary of only what it chose to report. It can miss, misread, or state a belief as fact. Verify findings before acting and read the source yourself when the detail decides. One question, one answer; the process exits afterwards.

question.description: The local question to investigate, with scope and the evidence you need.

tools.name: research
tools.description: Ask a cheap intern to research external sources, documentation, APIs, or libraries; optionally supply material to read. A cheap intern is fast and keeps reading out of your context, but returns a lossy summary of only what it chose to report. It can miss, misread, or state a belief as fact. Verify findings before acting and read the source yourself when the detail decides. One question, one answer; the process exits afterwards.

question.description: The question to investigate, including the version or constraints that matter.

material.description: Sources, URLs, excerpts, or background to read alongside the question.

tools.name: ledger_add
tools.description: Create one new timestamped .ledger task bundle with task.md, retrospective.md, and a live index row. Add plans, specifications, notes, decisions, evidence, or assets later only when useful. Not for listing, inspecting, selecting, updating, closing, or executing existing tasks.

description.description: One-line search summary, 1-400 characters. Stored on the live index row and carried into history.

slug.description: Optional lowercase kebab slug. Defaults to a slug derived from the title.

tools.name: ledger_status
tools.description: Move one live .ledger task to a new status. planning, ready, and in-progress update Status in task.md and on the live index row. done and cancelled archive the bundle into .ledger/history and move the row to the history index; call them only after edits to the bundle are committed. Not for creating, inspecting, shaping, executing, or judging completeness.

task.description: Task id, .ledger/<id>, or .ledger/<id>/task.md of the live task.

status.description: New status. done and cancelled archive the task.

tools.name: wiki_lint
tools.description: Read-only validation of the project .wiki Obsidian page graph. Reports duplicate case-insensitive filename-stem slugs, unresolved or ambiguous page links, missing headings, and unsafe symlinks with source evidence. Output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50.0KB; full output is saved to a temp file when truncated.

tools.name: wiki_references
tools.description: Resolve a project .wiki Markdown page by case-insensitive filename-stem slug or .wiki-relative path, then return its directed inbound, outbound, or bidirectional page-link neighborhood to depth 1 or 2. Read-only. Output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50.0KB; full output is saved to a temp file when truncated.

target.description: Page slug or Markdown path relative to .wiki (a .wiki/... path is also accepted).

direction.description: Graph direction to traverse. Defaults to both.

tools.name: context_lint
tools.description: Read-only check of every context file under the project's `.context/` directory: orphaned context files, headings other than `## file` or `## symbol:<name>`, duplicate headings, symbols absent from the source file, missing `Coupled:` and `Verify:` paths, and `[[wiki-links]]` that name no .wiki page.

tools.name: send_mail
tools.description: Start an addressed conversation with one or more people; use reply to continue one. Mail pushes each new message to its current members. At-home recipients' mail waits for reopening. Names resolve in your organization; known foreign IDs work. Mail to operator waits in their inbox; ask_user_question interrupts now.

items.description: A name in your organization, a known session ID, operator, my-team or my-manager.
A name in your organization, a known session ID, operator, my-team or my-manager.

cc.description: Copies become members and receive future replies.

tools.name: reply
tools.description: Continue an existing conversation in place. Mail and task replies push to current members. Channel replies stay pulled unless notify explicitly requests selected people's attention; names in prose are just text. Use send_mail for a new exchange, or post for shared channel context.

thread.description: The returned conversation ID; an ID alone grants no access.

items.description: A name in your organization, a known session ID, operator, my-team or my-manager.

notify.description: Explicit attention recipients who already have access. Names in prose do not notify. Channel-only.

tools.name: post
tools.description: Publish shared context in a channel you can access. Posts wait for catch-up; only notify requests selected people's attention. Names in prose are just text. Posting leaves following and unread history unchanged. Use invite_to_thread to grant an absent colleague access before notifying them.

channel.description: An accessible topic, team or organization channel ID.

items.description: A name in your organization, a known session ID, operator, my-team or my-manager.

notify.description: Explicit attention recipients who already have access. Names in prose do not notify. Channel-only.

tools.name: escalate
tools.description: Raise a decision, risk or blocker beyond your authority with your manager; at an organization root it goes to the operator's inbox. State what needs a decision, the evidence and your recommendation. This is mail, so continue unaffected work. Use ask_user_question for an immediate operator interruption.

body.description: The decision needed, evidence and recommendation.

tools.name: inbox
tools.description: List your addressed conversations and followed channels with unread messages. Use all:true for read threads too, and find_channels to discover channels you do not follow. Entries include unread counts, lifecycle and current-context references. This is a preview; read_thread with view:catch_up advances catch-up.

all.description: Include read and archived conversations too. Unread final messages appear even without this flag.

limit.description: Requested page size; no implicit history budget.

cursor.description: Opaque continuation from this query; preserves its original filters/view.

tools.name: create_channel
tools.description: Create a topic channel for shared context without changing reporting or assignments. People in its recorded organization scope can discover, read and post. Creation follows it; optional invite records persistent explicit grants and follows it for named colleagues. Creation is quiet and launches nobody. Use group mail for an addressed private exchange.

name.description: Channel label; use find_channels to check existing context first.

purpose.description: What belongs in this shared context.

items.description: A name in your organization, a known session ID, operator, my-team or my-manager.

invite.description: People to invite to retained history; grants persist across later scope changes.

tools.name: find_channels
tools.description: Discover channels you can access by name or purpose, including ones you do not follow. Results show recorded scope, following, archive state and the pinned current-context reference. Discovery neither follows nor reads history. Use inbox for your unread conversations and directory to find people.

archived.description: Defaults to exclude; archived channels remain accessible and joinable.

limit.description: Requested page size; no implicit history budget.

cursor.description: Opaque continuation from this query; preserves its original filters/view.

tools.name: join_channel
tools.description: Follow an accessible channel so activity appears in catch-up lists. Joining neither requests attention nor acknowledges history, starts a process or accepts work. It creates no access grant. Use invite_to_thread when someone needs access; a channel ID alone is not an invitation.

channel.description: An accessible channel ID, including an archived channel.

tools.name: leave_thread
tools.description: Leave an addressed conversation, or stop following a channel. For mail, leaving removes membership and future replies. For a channel, it only removes it from catch-up lists: access and explicit notifications remain possible. Neither changes assignments or reporting. Use remove_thread_invitation to remove an explicit grant; task audiences stay work-owned.

thread.description: The returned conversation ID; an ID alone grants no access.

tools.name: invite_to_thread
tools.description: Invite people into retained conversation history. In mail they become members and receive future replies. In a channel an explicit grant persists across scope changes, even if access already exists, and follows it for them. Invitations are quiet and change neither staffing nor assignments. Known foreign IDs work; task audiences stay work-owned.

thread.description: The returned conversation ID; an ID alone grants no access.

items.description: A name in your organization, a known session ID, operator, my-team or my-manager.

people.description: People to invite; this exposes retained history, not just future posts.

tools.name: remove_thread_invitation
tools.description: Remove explicit channel invitations or addressed-conversation members. Organization-derived access remains; results report effective access and following separately. tools.name: link
tools.description: Record a relationship between two things, or resolve one by id. Name each thing as kind:id with kind one of task, person, thread, message, commit, pr, file, check, organization (a task by id or ledger path, a person by name or id, a commit by SHA, a PR by URL, a file by path, a check run by its command and time or CI URL, the organization by its root's id). Relations: blocks: The first cannot go on until the second is done. requires_decision: The first waits on a decision the second must make. produced: The first produced the second: a commit, a PR, a file, or another result. verifies: The first, a check run or a review, verifies the second. supersedes: The first replaces the second; nobody's fitness changes. predicts: The first, a message stating a change, holds a scenario forecasting the second's fitness. fixes: The first fixes a defect in the second, earlier work. finds: The first found a problem in the second; the second's owner resolves it accepted or rejected. A wait (blocks, requires_decision) on a task ends on its own when that task closes done; resolve any other link yourself. A finds link targets a task; its owner resolves it accepted or rejected as evidence, never value. Any link can carry data.impact: {dollars: number, kind: 'incurred' | 'estimated', at?: epoch milliseconds}. Only incurred impacts enter economic accounting, at that time or link creation. Record actual losses or gains, never avoided losses or value/cost already counted; impacts are assertions the substrate does not verify. A predicts link from the message stating a change to organization:<root> stores unchanged forecast premises in data.scenario. Record before acting; keep hypothetical impacts nested inside data.scenario, not top-level data.impact.

id.description: Resolve this link instead of recording one.

resolution.description: With id: a word for how it ended, such as accepted or rejected.

reason.description: A short reason or evidence reference.

data.description: Structured data; scenario: forecast premises for a predicts link. impact: {dollars: number, kind: 'incurred' | 'estimated', at?: epoch milliseconds}. Estimates are listed, not charged.

inferred.description: True when you infer the relationship rather than know it.

confidence.description: With inferred: how sure you are, 0 to 1.

tools.name: economics
tools.description: Compare recorded value, delay and compute in dollars over a past window. This is optional economic comparison beside progress, bottlenecks, coordination and experience, not a compulsory objective. Shows totals/rates, task/person/link contributions, incurred impacts, finding records and unvalued coverage. Estimates and findings are evidence, not charges. Dropped-work spend explains costs already counted on currently cancelled/replaced tasks, possibly classified after the window; it is not extra cost or a waste verdict. Temporary-peer spend follows immutable ancestry to a lasting caller under event-time membership; missing legacy callers and spans stay unknown. New peers have recorded zero baselines; legacy first-sight spend remains a baseline. Task compute uses accounting-person focus as an estimate, including caller focus for peers; absent/ineligible focus stays unattributed. Subtree filtering narrows contributions, not organization totals. Alternatively give scenarios alone for probability-weighted comparison through the same evaluator. Scenarios require identical decision point, horizon, opportunity/task identities, valuations and starting histories; their premises are supplied assumptions, not measured benefits or certified live snapshots. Times are millisecond offsets. decisionAt:'recording' binds preview now and a separately recorded prediction at link creation. Use predictions for qualified calibration, not causal proof.

Boring code is usually preferable to clever code. Cleverness spends maintenance attention every time somebody has to understand it again.
Code should be self explanatory when well written, comments are for extreme cases where the code truly cannot express its intent or operation.
Do not introduce abstractions in anticipation of a second implementation, a future configuration need, or some hypothetical reuse. Let the second real case justify the abstraction.
Do not make configurability out of constants that do not presently vary and do not create extension points before something actually needs to extend.
If an effort is greenfield, do not create migrations, compatibility layers, multiple versions, fallback paths, or other scaffolding as requirements evolve. Iterating on existing code can be greenfield if it has no consumers. This is more common than you think. Ask your user if you are unsure.

# Repository guide for agents

This file applies to the entire repository. It is a durable map and operating guide, not a copy of the user manual or a catalogue of every current symbol. Prefer the linked source of truth when details disagree.

## Read this first

Before changing anything:

1. Run `git status --short --branch` and preserve all existing work. This repository is often developed through multi-file architectural changes; do not assume a dirty tree is disposable.
2. Read `README.md` for the package catalog and install path (`docs/setup.md` covers a from-scratch Pi setup), then the relevant `docs/` page for product behavior and feature boundaries.
3. Read `docs/development.md` for module and formatting conventions.
4. If the work is governed by `.ledger`, read `.ledger/INDEX.md`, the selected task's `task.md`, and every active record it references. Resolve closed dependencies through `.ledger/history/`. See `docs/ledger.md` for the workbench model.
5. Inspect the manifest and test configuration before adding a new path. Packaging, TypeScript, Vitest, and the extension loader each have explicit inclusion boundaries.

Authority is split deliberately:

- `package.json` is the machine-readable package, extension, skill, script, engine, and dependency contract.
- `README.md` is the human catalog and install path.
- `docs/` owns user-facing feature contracts. `docs/boundaries.md` records adopted and deliberately rejected ideas.
- `docs/development.md` owns coding and module conventions.
- `docs/ledger.md` owns the durable `.ledger` workflow.
- Tests own executable invariants, but a test can still encode an obsolete contract; compare it with current product documentation and instructions.
- This file explains how those pieces fit together. Keep it conceptual so ordinary feature additions do not require updating it.

## What this repository is

`apple-pi` is one installable Pi package that composes Alex's coding-agent environment. It is not an application server and not a monorepo of separately published packages. The root manifest is the only package boundary; directories under `components/` are internal source organization.

At a high level, the package adds seven kinds of capability to Pi:

1. **Turn assistance and interaction** — a persistent read-only pair programming partner that can ask colleagues for second opinions by mail, a structured user-question tool, and one reflection on the agent's own edits before a run finishes.
2. **Context continuity** — Pi native LLM summarization with a fail-closed automatic-compaction gate, the pair programmer's sourced notebook, two complementary session-recall paths, and a project-local wiki for reusable knowledge.
3. **Execution continuity** — root-session background work, one-shot reminders, and reactive command monitoring, plus the ledger for durable operational memory.
4. **Execution and team collaboration** — a bounded, type-checked Monty Python composition runtime that can give turns to peers, two one-shot intern tools (explore, research), and an organization of lasting peer sessions hired into roles, who work through mail threads, team channels, meetings, escalation, and assigned tasks.
5. **Workflow guidance** — packaged skills for review, ledger task lifecycles, and fresh-context Ralph loops, plus explicit prompt templates such as proposal-first promotion.
6. **Integration bridges** — Pi-native MCP in root sessions, plus provider-specific hosted-tool injection for supported xAI requests and a priority service tier toggle.
7. **Terminal and session ergonomics** — custom input editor, terse tool rendering, prompt stashing, RTK command rewriting, macOS completion notifications, automatic human session names, and a tmux agent sidebar and dashboard.

The design goal is an integrated Pi environment with one implementation of each responsibility. Features that are intentionally delegated to Pi or a dependency should not be copied locally.

## Runtime mental model

Pi discovers the package through the `pi` section of `package.json`. Each configured extension entrypoint installs tools, commands, event hooks, renderers, or provider hooks into Pi. Most files under `extensions/` are thin integration wrappers over cohesive code in `components/`. ledger is a deliberate exception: its small add/close/prompt integration lives in `extensions/ledger.ts`, while the shared contract text and lifecycle procedures live with their actual consumers rather than behind a ledger domain component.

There are four kinds of execution context to keep distinct:

- **Root Pi session** — every person in the organization: a session the operator started, a hired or reopened peer, and a temporary peer a program started (in a tmux window of the caller's server, or a headless RPC process outside tmux). Each discovers the package extensions: the session-state bridge and workplace tools, interns, `pi_exec`, tasks, the pair programmer, and the rest. Organizational insights and peer delegation follow the role's `manages` capability, with an exception for unroled recorded organization roots. The full management job charter stays exclusive to managing roles; general task links, mail and ordinary composition are available to every person. People reach each other only through the session-state runtime, never through an in-process parent.
- **Intern process** — one headless `pi --mode json --print --no-session` run per `explore` or `research` call, owned by `components/interns/src/runner.ts`. It does not discover package extensions; it loads automatic-compaction safety, vroom (fast mode), the search root guard, ledger, wiki, code context, and `search_session` by explicit path, with only the reading built-ins (shell included, `edit` and `write` excluded), wiki tools, and `context_lint`. It has no session-state bridge, organization identity, interns, or `pi_exec`, so it cannot delegate. It answers once and exits.
- **`pi_exec` guest** — runs type-checked Python in Monty subprocesses with an explicit bridge to Pi tools. It does not receive ambient Node filesystem or process authority. It can call core and extension tools through Pi's tool pipeline, fetch, evidence helpers, saved programs, and peers (attached colleagues or temporary catalog-role people, each a root session above), and its Monty state follows Pi's session tree. Root-only `remind_me`, `monitor`, and `task` remain outside the guest.
- **Internal sessions** — in-memory SDK sessions a root owns: the private `/btw` conversation (loads only automatic-compaction safety, vroom, and the search root guard, with read-only tools) and the pair programmer's sidecar (no package extensions; its tools are supplied by the pair integration). Forked continuations (change and learning reflection) are headless forks of the root's own conversation. None of these is a person or has a directory row.

When debugging a missing tool or duplicated lifecycle effect, first establish which of these contexts is executing.

## Core flows and invariants

### Package and extension loading

- The package ships source ESM. The exceptions are `components/browser-pages/dist/`, the browser pages built from `components/browser-pages/web/` with `npm run build:web`, and `apps/agent-workplace/dist/`, built with `npm run build:workplace`; both are committed because Pi installs git packages without dev dependencies.
- TypeScript uses NodeNext semantics, and relative TypeScript imports use `.js` suffixes because that is the runtime ESM path.
- The root manifest's extension list, skills and prompt paths, published `files` allowlist, and dependency declarations are part of the product surface.
- Native harness capabilities teach their concise selection, mental model, and ordinary composition patterns through runtime prompt-bearing surfaces: tool names, schemas, prompt snippets/guidelines, or explicit system-prompt injection. Repository documentation is invisible to the running model and never satisfies this requirement. Skills own repeatable engineering procedures and optional progressive disclosure; they are not prerequisite manuals for calling native tools.
- A model-called tool takes arguments the model writes, often from what the user suggests. Teach it through the tool's description and guidelines, and add a parallel human command or flag parser only when the operator asks for one.
- The package-load test is the executable smoke test for loading the manifest's extension entrypoints from the checkout and checking the expected tool/command boundary. It does not load the packed tarball, so inspect packaging separately.

### Context and notebook

- **Pi owns compaction** for every provider and the private pair session through its native LLM summarizer (see `docs/context.md`). apple-pi leaves authentication, history retention and summary generation with Pi. The notebook appends one persisted packet of current conclusions after each compaction; it supplements the summary and never rewrites request context per turn.
- Passive, automatic prompts that make the model act run as forked continuations (`components/shared/src/forked-continuation.ts`, `docs/forked-continuations.md`): a headless fork of the identical conversation returns one message that joins the stack without a steer or continuation. Prompts and commands the user starts stay in-band.
- Request context is append-only. A `context` hook that removes, reorders, or rebuilds a message on each request breaks provider prefix caching for the whole history; `tests/context-hooks.test.ts` allowlists the only hook that may filter. `npm run audit:cache` (`scripts/cache-audit.mjs`) reads real Pi session logs; run it after a context change to confirm that prefix caching still works.
- Use Pi's native compaction instead of a local compiler or provider-compaction replacement. The notebook adds only jointly curated conclusions, not a second conversation summary.
- `search_session`, `revisit_note`, and pair receipt expansion are intentionally separate: the first progressively searches transcript/file-operation history, the second follows a known notebook entry back to its source evidence, and receipts reveal only folded historical content already presented to the pair. The pair receives the latter two, not general session search.
- The pair programmer's notebook is authoritative in Pi's append-only session JSONL. Receipt handles are ephemeral capabilities scoped to one pair store and the active primary lineage; expanded payloads preserve their original source-entry provenance. Do not add a project-local mirror without an explicit storage, privacy, merge, and migration design.
- Reload, switch, fork, and shutdown paths matter. Any asynchronous work holding a Pi extension context must stop or re-prime when that context becomes stale.

### Exec, interns, and peers

- `pi_exec` is a bounded composition bridge, not an unrestricted Python interpreter. Preserve call, concurrency, memory, output, and time limits; preserve cancellation and durable nested-operation traces. Peer turns count against the agent budget.
- Guest APIs take explicit serializable arguments. New capabilities should cross a deliberate host bridge and participate in budgeting, tracing, and cancellation.
- Extension tools are reached through `ctx.tools`/`ctx.executeTool()`, but provider-private behavior that is not represented as a Pi tool is not automatically available.
- Three ways to hand work on, with separate owners: interns (`components/interns/`) for one-shot reading, peers in the organization (`components/organization/` and the session-state runtime) for lasting work, and `pi_exec` for programmatic composition, whose model turns run on peers. Do not add a fourth delegation runtime, an in-process child manager, or user-defined agent types; a new kind of person is a role in `roles/`.
- Interns and internal sessions do not discover package extensions; each loads an explicit list (see the execution contexts above). Recursion is prevented because none of them loads the interns, `pi_exec`, or the session-state bridge. Interns omit `edit` and `write`; read-only behavior is otherwise an instruction, not a sandbox.
- Peers are root sessions with their own transcripts. A program attaching a colleague waits for it to be idle and never closes or retires it; temporary peers get an assigned ephemeral task and are discarded (record deleted, transcript kept) when their call or the execution ends, fails, or is cancelled. The runtime, not `pi_exec`, owns their processes.
- Notebook ownership and curation stay with the root session and its pair programmer. Interns, programs, and internal sessions do not write another session's notebook.
- Avoid global registries unless they are explicitly process-scoped integration points with lifecycle cleanup.
- Nested `pi_exec` calls to extension, MCP, and active core tools other than `bash` go through Pi's tool pipeline, so `tool_call`/`tool_result` hooks see them with `parentToolCallId`. Programs' own `bash`, inactive core tools, fetch, evidence helpers, and peer turns do not; a policy that must gate those treats `pi_exec` itself as the capability boundary.
- Every lasting session is a Pi session with its own JSONL transcript. Do not add a second transcript or memory store for delegation or the workplace; threads and assignments live in the session-state runtime.

### The ledger, review, and Ralph

- The ledger is a simple project-local convention: `.ledger/` contains one open-ended directory per undertaking. The repository owner decides whether it is ignored, committed, or shared.
- `.ledger/INDEX.md` maps live tasks; closed bundles move unchanged under `.ledger/history/`. Continue an existing task when it already owns the undertaking.
- A new task contains only `task.md` and `retrospective.md`. Skills and operators may add any useful files or directories inside the bundle; the workflow that creates an artifact owns its format, not the ledger. Existing task bundles remain valid.
- `retrospective.md` distills what mattered and lessons worth retrieving without replaying the operational record. Promote durable lessons to their real owner when appropriate.
- `ledger_add` creates a task and index entry in `planning`. `ledger_status` moves it between `planning`, `ready`, and `in-progress`, or archives it as `done` or `cancelled` without judging completeness. Read and edit existing task files with ordinary repository tools.
- Repository documentation and tests retain durable product authority; task-specific execution context stays in the ledger.
- Captured code reviews are durable jobs in the existing session-state runtime. Its worker reuses ordinary peer lifecycles; the code-review skill guides intent, risk and evidence rather than requiring a board or implementing another engine. Ralph remains a skill over `pi_exec`.

### External integrations

- MCP protocol, transport, authentication, resources, UI, and native discovery belong to Pi. Apple Pi does not install an adapter or register `/mcp`; internal sessions omit the native factories.
- `pi_exec` is the composition runtime. Interns and internal sessions do not load Pi's native `codemode`, and `docs/mcp.md` recommends disabling it in the root session; do not reintroduce it as a parallel lane.
- Provider-specific payload hooks must be narrowly gated by provider/API and idempotent when a caller already supplied the capability.
- Third-party provenance and licensing belong in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`; do not edit vendored `node_modules/` source.

`docs/boundaries.md` records adopted and deliberately rejected ideas. Consult it before restoring an absent feature: absence is often an architectural choice, not unfinished work.

## Where a change should go

Use the narrowest production owner:

- Pi registration or event wiring: `extensions/`.
- Domain behavior with independent tests: the owning `components/<domain>/src/` tree.
- Terminal rendering for a component: that component's `ui/` modules.
- Logic used by multiple real subsystems with identical semantics: `components/shared/`.
- User-facing package behavior and configuration: the relevant `docs/` page. Keep `README.md` as the catalog and install path.
- Deferred and reactive root-session execution: `components/tasks/`; keep reminders one-shot and relative, keep monitor stdout line-oriented and steering, reuse the managed-task lifecycle, and keep `remind_me`, `monitor`, and `task` outside Pi Exec.
- RTK command rewriting and prompt injection: `components/rtk/` for detector, rewriter, and prompt; `extensions/rtk.ts` for the prompt section (rewriting lives in `components/tasks/src/bash-tool.ts`).
- Stable maintainer conventions or architecture rationale: `docs/`.
- organization behavior: roles, souls, selves, charters, and the directory in `components/organization/`; a new role is a Markdown file in `roles/`; the tree, threads, assignments, and their facts in the session-state runtime; the workplace tools in `components/session-state/src/` (manager tools in `coordinator.ts`); the contract in `docs/organization.md`. Do not add a roster file, a role-change path, a handoff schema, or caps.
- ledger behavior: keep add/status/prompt wiring in `extensions/ledger.ts`, shared contract text in `components/shared/src/ledger-system-prompt.ts`, lifecycle procedures in their owning descriptively named skill directories, and semantics in `docs/ledger.md`. Do not recreate a ledger domain component, parser/catalog, operations hub, or active-task pointer without an explicit new product contract.
- wiki behavior: keep derived Markdown graph logic and compact prompt/tool registration in `components/wiki/` plus `extensions/wiki.ts`, mutation procedures in `skills/llm-wiki/`, and product semantics in `docs/wiki.md`. Do not add a stored graph, cache, watcher, registry, or wiki mutation tool without a concrete new failure.
- Repeatable agent procedure: `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and, when needed, its local `references/`.
- Explicit user-invoked model workflow that needs no runtime state: `prompts/<command>.md`.
- Task-specific investigation, decisions, or evidence: the governing `.ledger` bundle, not production code.

Do not add metadata, fixtures, schemas, loaders, or policy modules without identifying the production consumer and the incorrect behavior prevented by the addition. Avoid compatibility wrappers, duplicate implementations, dormant toggles, speculative abstractions, and “new/v2” paths unless a real migration contract requires coexistence.

## Development setup

Use the root package only:

```bash
npm install
```

For a clean reproducible checkout, `npm ci` is appropriate. Follow the Node engine declared in `package.json`.

Install the checkout into Pi using the command documented in `README.md` when exercising the package interactively. Do not publish, globally install, or change project activation as part of routine validation unless the operator authorizes it.

## Validation commands

The normal proof sequence is:

```bash
npm run format:check
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run pack:check
```

Useful narrower commands are defined in `package.json`:

- `test:unit` runs Vitest suites for components and root integration.
- `test:pair` runs the pair's offline Node harness and expects the `pi` executable on `PATH`; its networked E2E mode is opt-in.
- `test:loader` loads the manifest's extension entrypoints from the checkout and checks the exposed surface.
- `pack:check` prints npm's dry-run package contents. Inspect that list for expected source; the command does not assert completeness or test the tarball in an installed environment.
- `program_rpc_smoke` (`.pi/programs/rpc_smoke.py`) sends one prompt through the real installed Pi in RPC mode in a temporary directory and reports custom messages and usage. Use it to check root-session behavior that the faux-model tests cannot, such as prompt caching. It calls the real default model.

Run the cheapest falsifying check while iterating, then the full relevant suite before declaring completion. A passing unit suite does not prove package loading, and a successful package dry run does not prove behavior. Some session-search tests write temporary session JSONL; they must not touch real Pi session files.

`npm run format` writes across broad repository paths. In a dirty working tree, prefer formatting only files you changed (for example with Biome's path arguments), then run the non-writing repository check. Never use a blanket formatter as accidental cleanup of someone else's work. RTK rewrites `npx biome format --write <paths>` into a command that reports success but writes nothing; run formatters that write files with `verbatim: true`.

RTK output can also report a commit that did not land. After each commit, confirm it with `git log --oneline -1` and `git reflog -3` run with `verbatim: true` before staging more work.

Other lanes (the operator or other agents) edit this checkout during long runs. Commit whole files of your own work, without partial-hunk staging; slight overlap with another lane is acceptable, and their remaining files stay unstaged. When a file you own changes unexpectedly, read its test diff as well as its code diff: a green suite can hide a test that was rewritten to stop exercising a case.

When adding a new source or test area, inspect all of these inclusion points:

1. `package.json` published `files` and Pi entry configuration.
2. `tsconfig.json` includes.
3. `vitest.config.ts` test includes, or the dedicated non-Vitest runner.
4. `tests/package-load.mjs` if the public runtime surface changes.
5. Formatting/lint script paths in `package.json`.

A file that works from the checkout but is absent from the package tarball is a release defect.

## Coding conventions

- Use strict TypeScript and ESM. Keep `.js` suffixes on relative imports.
- Follow `.editorconfig`: tabs for code; spaces for Markdown, JSON, and YAML; LF; final newline; no trailing whitespace.
- Biome is the formatter and linter. Do not hand-format against it or weaken rules to make a change pass.
- Keep extension-facing `index.ts` files thin. Re-export a small public surface and delegate installation or behavior to a cohesive owner.
- Split modules at a production consumer, test seam, or one-way dependency boundary—not merely because a file is long.
- Keep state machines cohesive when splitting would hide lifecycle ownership. Existing complexity suppressions should name the specific cohesive boundary they protect.
- Use Typebox for Pi tool schemas and keep runtime validation aligned with the declared schema.
- Preserve structured cancellation and error visibility. Do not turn failures into success-shaped defaults or broad catches.
- Add comments for durable, non-obvious constraints (trust boundaries, lifecycle ordering, protocol shape), not to narrate a diff.

### Adding or changing an extension surface

1. Identify the owning component and keep registration thin.
2. Add or update the extension entrypoint.

4. Test domain behavior directly.

### Changing exec, intern, or peer behavior

1. Decide whether the behavior belongs to one-shot reading (interns), program composition (`pi_exec`), or the organization's peers and workplace (session-state runtime).
2. Verify root-session, intern-process, and program-peer behavior separately.
3. Preserve tool scope, serialization, budgeting, cancellation, trace recovery, usage accounting, and cleanup.
4. Test both success and the relevant failure boundary; use integration tests when subprocesses or nested tool calls are involved.

### Adding, changing, or removing a skill

1. Keep the trigger precise so the skill is not loaded for unrelated work.
2. Put reusable long examples or role prompts in that skill's `references/` directory.
3. Keep runtime code in production modules; skills instruct agents but are not hidden application state.
4. Before removing a skill, inventory its mental models, selection rules, procedures, and examples. Migrate anything required for ordinary native capability use into an always-present runtime prompt surface; documentation is not a substitute.
5. Verify package inclusion and any loader/integration invariant that depends on the skill, and assert retained runtime guidance in tests when removing one.

### Importing third-party work

1. Adopt behavior intentionally rather than copying an entire upstream architecture.
2. Keep one local implementation of each responsibility.
3. Record source and license provenance.
4. Update `docs/boundaries.md` only when the durable architectural decision changes. Update the README catalog only when the public surface changes.
